# What does holding a position cost?

*You'll need position limits (chapter 2), the fair value and the wall mid (chapter 3), take, clear and make and the
round trip (chapter 4), and adverse selection (chapter 5). The fill rules `all` and `worse` are named here and
explained in chapter 10.*

## The story

Run the template on Prosperity 3's round 1 and look at its position in Kelp, the product whose price wanders. It is
long most of the day. Over the three days its mean position is between +21.5 and +35.2 lots, depending on the day
and on the fill rule (`all`, `worse`, or orders that rest), out of a limit of 50, and it sits at the limit itself on 5 to 15% of ticks
[(`IDEAS.md`, "`skew` against Kelp's long position"; `experiments.study.kelp_drift`)]{.src}.

That looks like a market maker failing at its one job, staying flat. The textbook fix is a *skew*: move both quotes
down when long, so the bot buys less and sells more. First we asked a plainer question. Is something in the bot leaning long, or is the market handing it a long position?

The test was to mirror each day. Every price is reflected around the day's middle, so each rise becomes a fall; every
bid becomes an ask; every buyer in the trade record becomes a seller. If the bot has a bias, a fair value that sits a
little low or quotes that lean one way, it stays long on the mirrored day. If the position comes from the flow, it
flips. It flipped exactly: on day −2 a mean of +27.8 lots became −27.8, and the PnL was 6,724 credits on both days,
to the unit (@fig-mirror). The same held on every day, under `all`, under `worse` and with resting orders
[(`data/mirror_summary.csv`; `IDEAS.md`, "`skew` against Kelp's long position")]{.src}.

![The template's Kelp position on Prosperity 3's round 1, day −2, and on the same day mirrored: top, the price and its
reflection; bottom, our position. Data: `data/mirror_test.csv`, from `experiments.study.kelp_drift`'s `mirrored` and
the engine.](../figures/g07_mirror_test.png){#fig-mirror
fig-alt="Two panels over one day. Top: Kelp's price rises from 2,000 to about 2,028, and its mirror falls from 2,020 to about 1,992. Bottom: our position mostly between 0 and plus 50 lots on the real day, and the exact mirror image, between 0 and minus 50, on the reflected day; the mean is plus 27.8 against minus 27.8 lots, and the profit 6,724 credits on both."}

So the bot is symmetric, and the long comes from the people trading with it. Only 34 to 36% of Kelp's trades at the
touch are buys (41 to 43% of the volume), against about half on Resin, so the bot buys 1.24 to 1.32 lots passively for
each lot it sells. Then we tried the fix anyway. Every tick of skew cost money. This chapter is about why.

## The idea

### A position is a bet nobody chose

A market maker's position isn't a decision. It is what is left when the fills on one side outnumber those on the
other. Holding it costs in three ways.

- **It moves with the price.** A position of a given size gains or loses that many credits on every move of one.
  Kelp's price rose 28 credits over day −2; held at the day's mean position all day, the rise would have been worth
  about 780 credits, and a fall as much the other way. That is variance, not an expected loss.
- **It may come from informed traders.** If the traders who sold to us knew the price was about to fall, the
  position built from their trades loses on average. That is chapter 5's adverse selection, seen through the position
  instead of through each fill's markout.
- **It uses up the limit.** At +50 the bot can't buy. Every seller that would have hit its bid goes elsewhere, and
  half its business stops until the position comes down.

The second and third are expected costs: one a loss, the other income given up. The data can say whether the second
is there, and the third is small here, 5 to 8% of the time at a limit under the default fill rule. The first is a
risk, which costs something only if the score charges for risk.

### Skew: leaning the quotes

A dealer controls inventory with the tactics Harris tabulates: move both quotes against the position, quote more size
on the side that reduces it and less on the side that adds to it, take another trader's quote to change the position
at once, or hedge it in a correlated instrument [(Harris, Table 13-2, PDF p. 298)]{.src}. The template has the first
two as parameters and the third as its `clear` step; the hedge is chapter 8's. The price lever is `skew`:

::: {.eq speak="the template moves both quotes down by the skew times the position's gap from its target as a share of the limit, rounded to whole ticks"}
$$\text{shift} = \operatorname{round}\!\left(\text{skew} \times \frac{\text{position} - \text{target}}{\text{limit}}\right)$$
:::

So `skew` is the number of ticks both quotes move at the full limit: long 50 with `skew` 2, the bid drops two
ticks, so fewer sellers reach it, and the ask drops two, so more buyers do [(`python/bots/template.py:847`)]{.src}.
The target is zero unless a product has a reason to hold something, like a steady drift.

### Avellaneda–Stoikov in words

The famous version is Avellaneda and Stoikov's (2008). Their market maker is risk-averse: it maximises a utility of
its wealth at a known time T, when what it holds is valued at the mid. Its quotes centre not on the mid but on a
*reservation price*, its own value for the stock given what it already holds (equation 29, PDF p. 6; the same as equation 8,
p. 4):

::: {.eq speak="the reservation price is the mid, less the position times the risk aversion, times the price's variance, times the time left"}
$$r = s - q\,\gamma\,\sigma^2\,(T - t)$$
:::

Here [$s$]{speak="s"} is the mid, [$q$]{speak="q"} the position, [$\gamma$]{speak="gamma"} the risk aversion,
[$\sigma^2$]{speak="sigma squared"} the variance of the mid per unit of time, and [$T - t$]{speak="T minus t"} the
time left. A bigger position is more exposed, a jumpier price moves it further, and the longer it must be held, the
more the price can wander. Long, the reservation price sits below the mid, so both quotes drop: a skew. The spread is
then set around it, from the same risk term and from how quickly fills fall off with distance (equation 30).

Two later results reframe it. Guéant, Lehalle and Fernandez-Tapia, solving it with a position limit, showed
that the time left is an artefact of an approximation near the end: far from it, the skew is a constant times the
position (PDF pp. 8 and 11), which is the template's `skew`. Ahuja and co-authors put a mean-reverting price in place
of the random walk: far from the end, the best quotes are then constant around the long-run mean, and ignore the
inventory (PDF p. 8) [(`references/wiki/concepts/optimal-quoting-models.md`)]{.src}.

So the advice depends on its premises. The skew grows with the volatility of the *fair value*, the risk
that the thing you hold is worth less tomorrow. Where that is small, as on a pegged product, the theory asks for almost
no skew. And the whole model is built on a utility, a penalty on risk. A bot scored on profit alone has a risk aversion
of zero, and with none the reservation price is the mid: no skew at all.

### Is the position a signal or the flow?

The mirror test says the bot is symmetric. It doesn't say whether the long position is dangerous, because a mirrored
day mirrors the danger too. That needs Harris's test for informed counterparties, asked of the position: does it
predict the price moving against it? [(`references/wiki/concepts/informed-counterparties.md`)]{.src}

On Kelp it doesn't. The correlation of our position with the change in the price over the next 10 to 1,000 ticks is
between −0.10 and +0.18 over the three days and the three fill rules, mostly slightly positive. If the sellers knew
something, a long position would come before falls, and the number would be clearly negative
[(`IDEAS.md`, "`skew` against Kelp's long position")]{.src}.

The same answer comes out of the PnL. Split each tick's change in profit into two parts: what the fills earned at once,
and what the position earned by riding the price until the next tick. The second is the position times the next
change in the wall mid, summed over the day. On the three days it was +414, −71 and −518 credits, against total
Kelp profits of 6,724, 6,247 and 5,727. Over the three days, holding the position added −175 credits to 18,698: about
nothing. The rest is the spread [(`data/mirror_summary.csv`)]{.src}.

The split has to use the wall mid. Kelp's plain mid flickers around the walls from tick to tick (a lag-1
autocorrelation of −0.48, by `arena.diagnose`; chapter 3's flicker), so against it much of what the fills earned gets booked as the position's gain:
4,119 to 5,441 credits a day [(`data/mirror_summary.csv`, `riding_mid`)]{.src}. Chapter 3's noise reaches the
accounting too.

### Why the skew lost here

With the flow uninformed and the score in profit, a skew can only cost, and the figure below shows how much
(@fig-skew). Each tick of skew
gives up fills the bot would have had, and sells what it holds a little cheaper. In exchange the position shrinks: the
mean falls from +24.5 lots at no skew to +9.7 at 3 ticks under `all`. Kelp's profit falls with it, from 18,698 credits
to 15,893 at 3 and 11,324 at 8. Under `worse`, where fewer passive fills are counted, it falls faster, from 14,531 to
9,514 at 3 and 6,582 at 8 [(`data/skew_grid.csv`; `IDEAS.md`, "`skew` against Kelp's long position")]{.src}.

![Kelp's profit over the three days of Prosperity 3's round 1 against the template's `skew`, under both fill rules.
Data: `data/skew_grid.csv`, from `arena.grid ... --grid PARAMS.KELP.skew=0,1,2,3,4,6,8 --modes
all,worse`.](../figures/g08_skew.png){#fig-skew
fig-alt="Two falling lines. Under the optimistic rule Kelp makes 18.7 thousand credits at no skew, 15.9 thousand at 3 ticks and 11.3 thousand at 8. Under the strict rule 14.5 thousand, 9.5 thousand and 6.6 thousand."}

The theory's own coefficient does no better. Fitted from Kelp's volatility and fill rates, GLFT's closed form asks
for 0.6 ticks at the smallest risk aversion tried, 0.001, and costs 514 credits; at 0.01 it asks for 1.9 ticks and
costs 952 [(`data/glft_skew.csv`; `IDEAS.md`, "The skew coefficient from GLFT's closed form")]{.src}. And our engine,
like Prosperity, values the position left at the end at the mid, so holding to the close costs nothing extra.

### The skew a famous model prescribes

The textbook's case was tried by a team that knew it well. In Prosperity 4's round 1, DTU Quant Lab added an
Avellaneda–Stoikov skew to their market maker on Osmium, a product pegged at 10,000 with noise around it that reverts
quickly [(`references/prosperity4-dtu-quant-lab/README.md:85`)]{.src}. In
their backtest it cost 16,593 of that edition's credits (*their claim*), and they went back to a fixed fair value of 10,000
[(`references/prosperity4-dtu-quant-lab/README.md:91`)]{.src}.

Our grid on the same product agrees on the direction. Re-run today (the cited rows have older numbers from an earlier
template: 113.8 thousand at no skew and 93.4 at 8), over Prosperity 4's rounds 1 and 2, six days, the template's
Osmium makes 115.9 thousand credits with no skew, 115.5 thousand at 1 tick, 112.6 at 2, 107.1 at 4 and 96.0 at 8;
under `worse`, 115.9 thousand falls to 83.9. A fixed fair of 10,000, the mean-reverting model's constant quotes, makes
99.2 thousand with no skew and 53.6 thousand at 8 [(`data/osmium_skew.csv`; the wiki's `contradictions.md`, row 1)]{.src}.
GLFT's closed form, with the variance read off one-tick changes, asks for a skew of 94 ticks there even at a risk
aversion of 0.001, and makes 23.7 thousand, where the row's older run had 20 thousand against 114
[(`data/glft_skew.csv`)]{.src}. On a pegged price the one-tick variance is
noise, not risk: the model's premise, a price that wanders, doesn't hold. We didn't check which variance DTU used;
noise in the mid would explain their loss.

### The other levers, a line each

- **`size_skew`** shrinks the quote on the side that adds to the position, Harris's "change the sizes" (Bouchaud and
  co-authors' equation 17.4, PDF p. 342). On Kelp, 0 is best: 0.5 costs 91 credits and 4 costs 2,716. Verdict: `dropped here`
  [(`data/size_controls.csv`; `IDEAS.md`, "Inventory control through quote size")]{.src}.
- **`make_size`** caps each quote. A cap of 20 costs 3 credits on Kelp and nothing on Resin; 10 costs 903 and 625; 5 costs
  3,657 and 5,836. The flow a tick is smaller than the room, so the cap is no risk lever here: `dropped here` as one,
  kept for Pepper Root's drift bet against rivals [(`data/size_controls.csv`; `IDEAS.md`, "Using less than the full
  position limit")]{.src}.
- **`stop_loss`** flattens a product and stops it for the day once today's profit is that far below its high. It is
  meant for prices that leave, and chapter 7 shows how mixed that is on Prosperity 3: it does nothing when the fair
  value can't see the loss, and costs 17 to 20 thousand on some perturbed days when it can. Verdict: `kept`, set to about three
  times a product's largest plain-day drawdown [(`IDEAS.md`, "A loss stop per product")]{.src}.

All of these were measured on Prosperity's markets, so each verdict is a prior. The rows' re-test column asks this
chapter's question again: a skew only where Harris's test is clearly negative or the score charges for holding. The
day's list in On the Day, under "Every round", goes through that column.

::: {.callout-note title="What would differ on another market"}
On ABIDES the takers are informed: their trades move the price by 1.31 cents within 50 ticks (chapters 4 and 5), so a
position built from their fills comes before moves against it, the case the skew is for. We never measured a skew
there; the template loses on ABIDES before inventory matters. Inside `arena.sim`, a market that reacts to our orders,
a preset with Kelp's one-sided flow made the template 23.1 thousand credits against 21.2 thousand without it: flow
that knows nothing costs nothing there either [(`IDEAS.md`, "Replay against a market that reacts")]{.src}. Where the close is marked at a price the bot can't see, as in the Varde rehearsal (chapter 10), a position held to
the end carries a cost Prosperity never charged.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
Skew is a regulariser on the position: it trades expected profit for lower variance, and like weight decay it pays
only when the variance it removes would have cost you. The mirror test is an equivariance test: transform the input,
check the output transforms the same way. Where the analogy breaks: the data answer back, since skew changes who trades
with you, and a score that is a rank, not a profit, can make variance cost after all (chapter 13).
:::
